title: Sorting people by their stored surname puts "van der Berg" after "de Vries"; a Dutch phone book would put it before
assumption: Sorting a list of surnames alphabetically, exactly as the strings are stored, produces the one correct order.

input.description: A directory, address book, or customer list sorted by a 'last name' field that stores the full surname including any leading particle.

what_goes_wrong: Sorting the raw strings files "van der Berg" under V, after "de Vries"; the Dutch convention drops a leading particle (van, der, de) when computing the sort key, filing "van der Berg" under B, ahead of "de Vries" under V. The two conventions put these two names in a different relative order.
why: There is no single universal rule for sorting a surname with a leading particle. The Dutch convention, followed by Dutch directories and by library cataloging rules for Dutch names, drops the particle to compute the sort key; Belgian (Flemish) practice and many other systems keep it. A system that just lowercases and sorts the stored string whole keeps the particle in place. The conventions simply disagree, and most software picks the whole-string sort without ever deciding to.
affects: any 'sort by last name' feature using the raw stored string
library/bibliographic cataloging convention for particles (documented, not universally applied by software)

repros.expected_output:
['Bakker', 'de Vries', 'van der Berg']
['Bakker', 'van der Berg', 'de Vries']
False

[ 'Bakker', 'de Vries', 'van der Berg' ]
[ 'Bakker', 'van der Berg', 'de Vries' ]
false

fix: Pick a sort-key convention explicitly (whole string vs. particle-dropped) and apply it consistently, rather than sorting by whatever happens to be stored in the surname field, and don't assume there's one universally 'correct' convention; it varies by language and institution.

sources.title: Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names

test_cases.note: Decide and document which sort-key convention your directory uses for particled surnames; the two common ones disagree.
